<reason>Both sides were sharp, and CON deserves real credit for the most original moves in the debate: the selection dilemma ("parity would be underperformance"), the registry-generalizability point, and the strategic concession of custody/benefits/hospital protections to isolate the motion's empirical claim. But CON's route never squarely negated the motion as written. The motion asks whether children "do as well on average"; CON's own crystallization — "a rough wash between conceded advantages and conceded disadvantages" — describes outcome parity, which is PRO's claim, and PRO named that gap early ("parity is my claim"; policy responds to actual outcomes, not counterfactuals). CON also conceded, at every stage, no observed deficit. PRO converted CON's own analogy into its best turn: if the same research tradition reliably detects divorce and stepfamily effects, the instruments are sensitive enough that a policy-relevant gap would surface, which blunts the underpowered-null critique without overclaiming. PRO also honestly conceded that very small effects cannot be excluded and paired that with the fair point that no family form has passed the pre-registered equivalence test CON demands — turning CON's standard into a veto on evidence. CON's stigma/recognition line was cleanly turned into an argument for the policy limb rather than against it. Finally, CON's concession of the practical protections cut both ways: it made CON honest but shrank its opposed policy down to "courts shouldn't take judicial notice / research shouldn't be discouraged," which is a thin harm against PRO's concrete custody-and-hospital-room stakes. Execution notes: CON's opening was clipped for length, losing part of its policy limb; PRO's claim of continuing "silence" on opposed policy slightly overstated matters. Both handled Q&A with proper A1:/A2: labels and answered reasonably candidly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing dismantling of CON's late-named mechanism: biological separation is not caused by parental gender but shared with adoptive, donor-conceived, and remarried families, and the registry samples already contain precisely those children — so "the question was never asked" fails. Coupled with PRO's earlier turn of CON's own stepfamily example (the same instruments do detect real structural effects), this left CON with an epistemic worry but no located deficit.</best_rebuttal>
